stem: One full pass of bubble sort guarantees:
options: The LARGEST remaining value has bubbled to its final position at the end
explanation: Adjacent swaps carry the maximum rightward each pass - which is why the inner loop can shrink by one each time.

stem: The 'if (!swapped) break;' in bubble sort buys:
options: O(n) BEST case on already-sorted data - one calm pass proves it is done
explanation: A pass with zero swaps means sorted. Without the flag, bubble grinds its full quadratic work regardless.

stem: Insertion sort is genuinely the right choice for:
options: SMALL or NEARLY-SORTED arrays - O(n) when nearly ordered
explanation: The lesson measures it: ~0ms on 8,000 nearly-sorted items while selection grinds. Real sorts use it for small partitions.

stem: Selection sort is O(n squared) in EVERY case because:
options: It always scans the whole unsorted region for the minimum - luck cannot help it
explanation: Its one virtue: fewest swaps (n-1). Insertion exploits nearly-sorted input; selection cannot.

stem: The MERGE step combines two sorted halves by:
options: Repeatedly taking the SMALLER front item of the two
explanation: Two fingers walking two sorted arrays - O(n) per level, log n levels = O(n log n) in ALL cases. Concat-and-resort would wreck the complexity.

stem: After one quicksort PARTITION, the pivot is:
options: In its FINAL sorted position - smaller left, larger right
explanation: Each partition finally-places one element and splits the rest - recursion does the halves. Average O(n log n), in place.

stem: Last-element pivot on ALREADY-SORTED data gives quicksort:
options: O(n squared) - every partition is maximally lopsided
explanation: The pivot ends up at one extreme each time: n levels of n work. Middle or random pivots dodge it; introsort detects and switches.

options: Sorting by one key AFTER another - equal items keep their previous order (name within year)
explanation: Sort by name, then stably by year: names stay ordered within each year. Merge and OrderBy are stable; Array.Sort and selection are not.

stem: Quadrupling n made bubble ~16x slower but merge only ~4x. Because:
options: n squared grows 16x for 4x data; n log n grows ~4x - the gap only widens
explanation: The lesson's measured table: at a million items that is half an hour versus a quarter second.

options: INTROSORT: quicksort, switching to heapsort if recursion sours and insertion for small partitions
explanation: Best of three worlds - killing quicksort's worst case. In real code: Array.Sort or OrderBy, every time; the five classics are for understanding and exams.
